en: I am that Brahman alone, who, through the fire of the knowledge of equality, reduces to nothingness the delusion of the existence of anything other than myself— this is the Bhasmajābāla Upaniṣad.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
Hariḥ Oṃ.

Then Jābāla Bhusuṇḍa beheld Mahādeva, whose abode is the peak of Kailāsa, who is the very embodiment of Oṃkāra, who has Umā as the crest upon his head, whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, who possesses the luster of infinite moons and suns,
who wears a tiger-skin garment, holds a deer in his hand, and whose body is smeared with ashes.

His forehead shone with a horizontal triple-tilaka mark; he was the five-faced one, filled with smiles, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), immeasurable, without beginning or end, partless, devoid of qualities,
blissful, stainless, and free from affliction, uttering "huṃ phaṭ" and constantly chanting the names of Śiva.

Having bowed down again and again to the Blessed Lord Śiva— who has golden arms, a golden form, and a golden complexion; who is the treasure of gold, non-dual, the fourth state beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and the one object of refuge—
and having worshipped him repeatedly with bilva leaves and that sacred ash while prostrating his head, [he spoke].

With palms joined in reverence, he asked: "O Blessed One, having extracted the essence of the Vedas, please teach the procedure for the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), by means of which liberation is attained without looking to anything else.
What is the substance of the ash? What are the locations? And who are the sages (*manu*) in this regard?"

"How many are its recitations? Who are the qualified persons for this? What is their rule? Teach me, your disciple, liberation. Then the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, most compassionate, spoke even to the Pramathas and the gods:

Having inspected it, he should place the purified cow-dung in a leaf-vessel (*brahmaparṇa*) before sunrise in the morning and dry it with the mantra "tryambakam. Having established the fire there according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra* by means of whatever fuel is available, he should place that cow-dung substance therein.

Having placed [the materials], one should then offer oblations with sesame and rice grains mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), reciting the mantra "To Soma, svāhā! One thousand and eight, or five hundred, of these should be offered. In that rite, the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood;
by means of it, one does not hear evil. The mantra for that homa is simply "Tryambaka."
After the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the *pūrṇāhuti* is performed; by that same [procedure], the offering of oblations (*bali*) is made in the eight directions.

Having sprinkled those ashes with the *gāyatrī*, and having placed them in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, one should sprinkle them again with the *rudra-mantras* and establish them in a pure location.

Then one should feed the Brāhmaṇas; thereby one becomes purified oneself. Having gathered the ashes with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with "mā nastoke" and "sadyojāta," [one should apply them while reciting]: "The fire is ash, the wind is ash, the water is ash, the earth is ash, the ether is ash, the gods are ash."

"The seers are ash; indeed, all this is ash—purified, purifying, I bow to that which instantly destroys all sins. Having bowed with his head while reciting this, he places [the ash] in his purified left hand while reciting "To Vāmadeva," sprinkles it while reciting "Tryambaka," and [uses it] while reciting "The pure by the pure."
Having wiped and purified [the body], one should perform the smearing with that very ash from head to foot.
In this regard, there are five Brahma-mantras. Then follows the application of the remaining ash:
taking up the ash with the index, middle, and ring fingers while reciting "Agnir bhasmāsi" (The fire is the ash).
With "mūrdhānam," one should place [the mantra] on the crown of the head; with "tryambakam" on the forehead; with "nīlagrīvāya" on the throat; with "tryāyuṣam" on the right side of the throat;
with "vāmam" on the left side; with "kālāya" on the two cheeks; with "trilocanāya" on the two eyes; and with "śrotrayoḥ" on the two ears.
With the mantra "Śṛṇavāma" on the face, "Prabravāma" on the heart, "Ātmane" on the navel,
"Nābhi" on the root of the right arm, "Bhavāya" in its middle, "Rudrāya" at its wrist, "Śarvāya" on the back of that hand, and "Paśupataye" on the root of the left arm;

Having applied the ashes in sequence— saying "To Ugra" in the middle, "To Agre-vadhāya" at the wrists, "To Dūre-vadhāya" on the backs of the hands, "Obeisance to Hantr" on the shoulders, and "To Śaṅkara"—
and having bowed to Śiva saying "To Soma," one should then wash that ash with water.
One should drink [the water] with the mantra "punantu. It must not be discarded below; it must not be discarded below.

This ritual application of the sacred ash (bhasma-dhāraṇa) should be performed diligently according to the rules at the three times of day—midday and evening. Through negligence, one falls from grace. This alone is the dharma of Brahmins; this alone is [the dharma].

This is the law: one should not eat food, water, or anything else without having thus applied the sacred ash (bhasma). If, through negligence, one has abandoned the application of the sacred ash, one should not recite the Gāyatrī; one should not offer oblations into the fire, nor satisfy the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others.

This very dharma is eternal, the destroyer of all sins, and the cause of liberation. This dharma is obligatory for Brahmins—whether as students, householders, forest-dwellers, or renunciants. By failing to perform this, a Brahmin incurs sin. If one fails to do so through negligence, [one must recite it] one hundred and eight times.
By standing in the midst of water, reciting the Gāyatrī, and fasting for one day, one becomes pure.

A renunciant (yati), having abandoned the wearing of ashes, becomes pure by fasting for one day and reciting the Praṇava twelve thousand times. Otherwise, Indra [would deliver] the renunciants to the jackals.
He causes it to fall. If there is an absence of ash, then one must certainly wear other ash produced from the cremation of a virtuous man, purified by mantras.
One who employs this in the morning becomes purified from the sins committed during the night.

One is liberated from the theft of gold. Having performed the midday rite at noon, meditating until the end of the ritual worship, facing the sun and reciting, one becomes purified from the drinking of liquor; one becomes purified from the theft of gold.
One becomes purified from the killing of a Brahmin; one becomes purified from the killing of a cow;
one becomes purified from the killing of a horse; one becomes purified from the killing of a teacher;
one becomes purified from the killing of a mother; one becomes purified from the killing of a father.
One who employs this at the three times of day obtains the fruit of reciting all the Vedas; he enjoys the fruit of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*); being free from calumny, he reaches a full lifespan;
and he acquires the prosperity of Prajāpati, abundance of wealth, and mastery over cattle.
"Thus one should cause this Upaniṣad to revolve," said the Blessed Lord Sadāśiva with Ambā; [said] Sadāśiva with Ambā.
Thus ends the first chapter. || 1 ||

Then Bhusuṇḍa Jābāla, having prostrated before Mahādeva with Ambā, asked again: "What is it that must be performed daily by Brāhmaṇas, the non-performance of which causes a Brāhmaṇa to fall into sin? Who is to be worshipped? Or who is to be meditated upon? Who [is the Lord]?"

"How is he to be recollected? How is he to be meditated upon? Where is one to remain? Tell me this. He spoke to him briefly: "Having performed the purification rites and so forth before sunrise, one should then bathe;
the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) is with the *Rudra-sūktas*. Then one puts on unwashed clothing to ward off evil."

Meditating upon the rising sun, having smeared his limbs with ashes, he should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark in its proper place using white ashes alone and wear white *rudrākṣa* beads. This is not to be touched by others; likewise for others. He should wear forty beads on the head and one on the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

Or else, there are three [groups]: twelve on the two ears; thirty-two on the throat; sixteen on each of the two upper arms; twelve on each of the two wrists; and six on each of the two thumbs. Then, every day at the junctions of time (*sandhyā*), one should perform worship with *kuśa* grass and offer oblations into the fire with the mantras beginning with "Agni is light" (*agnir jyotiḥ*).

Having worshipped the Śivaliṅga at the three junctions of the day, sitting upon Kuśa grass, one should meditate upon me alone as Sāmba, mounted upon a bull, with golden arms, golden complexion, and golden form— the Puruṣa who releases beings from their bonds, dark-brown in hue, with upward-directed vital energy, and three-eyed.

Having consecrated with the Rudra-hymns Him who is of universal form, thousand-eyed, thousand-headed, thousand-footed, with arms on all sides, the soul of the universe, the one without a second, partless, actionless, peaceful, auspicious, imperishable, undecaying, the creator of Hari, Hara, and Hiranyagarbha, the immeasurable, without beginning or end;

With white ashes and *śrīphala* leaves—whether three-pronged and moist or dry—one should not touch [the deity] here. One should prepare the offerings for its worship as the sacrificial food (*naivedya*).
Thereafter, the eleven-fold *rudra* mantra is to be recited; the single-fold is the *ananta*. [The mantras are] the six-syllabled and the eight-syllabled.

Or the Śaiva mantra should be recited: one should utter "Oṃ" first, then "Namaḥ," followed by the three syllables "Śivāya. One should utter "Oṃ" first, then "Namaḥ," followed by the five syllables "Mahādevāya. There is no mantra superior to this Tāraka; this is the Tāraka.
The five-syllabled [mantra]. What is this Śaiva mantra? This Tāraka mantra is taught to the Śaiva souls in Avimukta. This very Śaiva mantra alone delivers;
it is itself the instruction of Brahman.
I am Brahmā, I am Soma, I am the Wind; I am Soma who blows,
I am Soma the progenitor of thoughts, I am Soma the progenitor of the earth,
I am Soma the progenitor of fire, I am Soma the progenitor of the sun— indeed, I am Soma.

I am the Soma generated by Indra; I am the Soma generated by Viṣṇu as well. I alone am the generator of that which belongs to the Moon, of the gods, and of all the worlds beginning with Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—the entire manifold world of beings.

That which has been born in many ways and that which is being born—of all this, I alone am the progenitor; I am Rudra, the Great Seer, who transcends the universe. I behold Hiraṇyagarbha and others as they are being born. I am Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, and who is in the plants.
Rudra, who has entered all beings, is exactly like this: he is this very Self, the inner Self, the light of Brahman. There is no one higher than me; I alone am the supreme, transcending the universe.
By knowing me alone, one attains immortality; by knowing me alone, one crosses over sorrow. By knowing me alone...

I dissolve the suffering of worldly existence; therefore, I am Rudra, who am the supreme goal of all. I am he who possesses all forms. From whom indeed these beings are born, by whom, once born, they live, and into whom they enter when they pass away—that is I alone.
Having known this, one should worship [Me]. Praised by the elements and by the gods, I alone am He of whom it is said: "From fear of Him the wind blows;
from fear of Him the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra, as well as Soma, proceed.
I am that very one who am the presiding authority over all and the source of all beings.
Pālaka: I am that earth; I am those waters; I am that fire; I am that wind; I am that time; I am those directions; I am the Self. Everything is established in me.
The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. May Brahman be Śiva unto me—Sadāśivom!
I am without eyes, yet possessing eyes everywhere; I am without ears, yet possessing ears everywhere; I am without feet, yet possessing feet everywhere;

I am without hands, yet possessing hands everywhere; I am without heads, yet possessing heads everywhere. My sole refuge is knowledge and mantra; I am the form of knowledge, I am composed of knowledge, I am the Lord of All, and I am ageless.

Having known Me thus, one is liberated from the bonds of transmigratory existence; therefore, I am the liberator from the bonds of the bound souls (*paśu*). The bound souls—those who dwell in the intermediate state up to the end of the non-human realms—and those whose minds are disciplined, strive to attain Me alone. Having attained Me, they do not return again.
Having taken refuge in Kāśī, which is situated upon the trident, even those who have abandoned their vital breaths enter into me alone.

Just as an oblation cast into a blazing fire does not reach the sacrificer, so too this [body], having abandoned the corpse, does not attain such a state as it did before. This indeed is the instruction; this...

This is the instruction: this alone is the supreme Dharma. One must never be negligent therein regarding truth, nor regarding the smearing with ashes (uddhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). Likewise, by wearing the Rudrākṣa beads and so forth, and by my worship; even through negligence, one should not void excrement within the temple of the Lord.
One must not neglect one's vows; for that indeed is austerity, that indeed is austerity, specifically for those desiring liberation in Kāśī.
It must not be abandoned, it must not be abandoned; I am the liberator for those dwelling in Avimukta. There is no place higher than Avimukta; there is no place higher than Avimukta.

In Kāśī there are four sites; among them, the inner apartment (antargṛha) is the most venerable. Even there, the Unliberated (Avimukta) is the most venerable. Within that, there are five sites; among them, the temple of Śiva (śivāgāra) is the most venerable. To the east of that is the site of sovereignty (aiśvaryasthāna).
In the south is the station of movement; in the west, the station of detachment;

in the north, the station of knowledge. Within that [station] is that which is internally untainted, imperishable, without beginning or end, known by all the Vedas and Vedāntas, indefinable, indescribable, immutable, desirable, and non-dual.

The support of all, yet without support, invisible, and served daily by the foremost of the immortals—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Purandara, and others—I alone am that Liṅga whose nature is light; I alone am to be worshipped, and that alone is to be worshipped.
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire, nor wind can conceive of that Liṅga.
That which is self-luminous, named Viśveśvara, presides over Pātāla;
that very one am I. There I am worshipped; I am worshipped directly by whoever, with mind fixed on me, honors me with radiant bilva leaves having three branches.

One who has offered the life-force to me, who has surrendered all actions to me alone, whose limbs are smeared with ashes, who is adorned with rudrākṣa beads, who has taken refuge in me alone with his whole being, and who is devoted solely to my worship— such a person should worship me. I eat that [offering].

I liberate him from the bonds of saṃsāra. By worshipping the Viśveśvara Liṅga there day after day, bathing it with the Rudra-hymns, and drinking three times that very water used for the ablution, one is liberated from great sins. Not... [is he not].

He incurs grief; he is liberated from the bonds of *saṃsāra*. Without honoring that [deity], one should not eat fruit, cooked food, or anything else. If one were to eat it, one would become a consumer of semen.
One should not drink water; if one were to drink it, one would become a consumer of pus. [This applies] even if done once through negligence.
Having failed to worship me, having eaten or fed [others], having had one's hair shaved,
or having taken up the five products of the cow, one should fast and perform the Rudra-bath in water.
One should recite the Rudrānuvāka three times while looking at and meditating upon the sun.
One should perform the purification with fierce mantras composed by oneself;
then, having fed the Brahmins, one becomes purified. Otherwise, after death, one undergoes torment. Having honored [the deity] with leaves, fruits, water, or other offerings...

Then, having consecrated me, the Lord of All (Viśveśvara), with the milk of a Kapila cow while reciting the Rudrasūkta, one becomes purified from the sin of killing a Brahmin by worshipping me alone in the form of the Śiva-linga. Having consecrated me with the clarified butter of a Kapila cow, one becomes purified from the theft of gold.

Having consecrated [the image] with honey, one becomes purified from the sin of approaching the wife of a guru. Having consecrated it with white sugar, one becomes purified from the sin of killing all living beings.
Having consecrated it with these substances such as milk and the rest, one attains all desires.
Thus, by worshipping each one with hundreds of measures of mahāprastha, using hundreds of measures of mahāprastha, one becomes liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra. [One should worship] me alone,
in the form of the Śiva-liṅga, on the day of Ārdrā, on the full moon, or on the new moon.

Or, having consecrated [the image] during a Mahāvyatīpāta yoga, an eclipse, or a solar transit, and having worshipped it with sesame seeds, rice grains, and barley; having honored it with bilva leaves; and having offered incense of *gandhasāra* mixed with *kāpila* ghee, one should present a lamp, an offering of food (*naivedya*), and a gift accompanied by ghee.

Having visualized [the deity], one should offer a handful of flowers. Thus, being self-restrained and having worshipped, one attains union (*sāyujya*) with me. Having performed an ablution with unbroken grains of rice (*akhaṇḍa-taṇḍula*) measuring a hundred *mahāprasthas*, one who desires the world of the Moon attains the world of the Moon. Having performed an ablution with that same quantity of sesame seeds, [one attains the world of Yama].

One who desires the world of Vāyu attains the world of Vāyu. Having been consecrated with this many beans, one who desires the world of Varuṇa attains the world of Varuṇa. Having been consecrated with this many barley grains, one who desires the world of Sūrya attains the world of Sūrya. Having been consecrated with twice as many of these, [one attains the world of Prajāpati].

One who desires the heavenly world attains the heavenly world. Having been consecrated with these fourfold qualities, one reaches the four-layered treasury of Brahman, which Death does not perceive. Having transcended that, one who desires the world of Māra attains the world of Māra; there is no other world beyond the world of Māra. Having attained it, one does not grieve.

He does not return again, he does not return again. Having fully worshipped me in the form of the *liṅga*, yogins, perfected ones, and those who have attained success meditate upon me; sacrificers sacrifice to me alone;
and the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, the Upaniṣads, and the Itihāsas, praise me alone.
There is nothing other than me; I alone am everything. Everything is established in me.
Therefore, I am to be worshipped daily by those who exert themselves at Kāśī. There, the hosts have fierce faces, various mouths, carry various weapons, and assume various forms.
Marked with various signs, they all have their limbs smeared with ashes and wear ornaments of rudrākṣa beads;
with palms joined in reverence, they constantly meditate upon me. There, in the eastern direction, Brahmā, with palms joined, worships me day and night. In the southern direction...

Viṣṇu, having placed his joined palms upon his head, worships me. In the western direction, Indra, with body bowed in reverence, worships me. In the northern direction, Umā—whose form is like fire, who is deeply enamored of me, adorned with golden ornaments, and clad in golden garments—worships me alone. Even the Vedas, assuming four forms, worship me. In the southern direction...

That place of liberation is known as the Muktimaṇḍapa (the Pavilion of Liberation). There, numerous Gaṇas, the Pālakas, armed and destroyers of sin, reside. There, the Śāmbhava, Pāśupata, and Mahāśaiva sages chant the five-syllabled Śaiva mantra, the crest-jewel of the Vedas, which is the liberating *tāraka*.

They remain there rejoicing with the utterance of the *praṇava*. Therein is a single jeweled altar (*ratnavedikā*). Seated there, I brought those who had abandoned their corpses at Kāśī, placed them upon my own lap, and having touched them while they were adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, I prayed: "May there be no further birth for these."
And death— I teach this *tāraka* mantra, which is the corpse. Then, liberated, they enter into me by means of their body consisting of pure consciousness (*vijñānamaya*),
and they do not return again, just as an oblation established in the fire remains right there.
This five-syllabled Śaiva mantra is taught for the sake of liberation;

that [mantra] is the locus of liberation. Beyond that is the form of Oṃ. Thereafter, for those whose actions are dedicated to Me and whose minds are permeated by Me, there arises the state of being My very self; this does not happen for others.

This is the knowledge of Brahman; this is the knowledge of Brahman. Those seeking liberation, seated in Kāśī alone, are vigorous and possessed of learning. [They enter] the sheath of Brahman consisting of consciousness, the four-layered sheath of Brahman, which Death does not perceive, which Brahmā [does not perceive].
He whom Viṣṇu does not perceive; whom Indra and Agni do not perceive;
whom Varuṇa and the others do not perceive—that very splendor, having consumed its state as semen, now dwelling in union with Umā in her golden form, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Those who meditate upon me, Śiva, thus— wearing the moon as a crown, with eyes of the moon, sun, and fire, and whose body is adorned with sacred ash— they become freed from sin, cast off their bonds,
and are absorbed into me alone; and so it is for others in the city of Kāśī who perform the act of voiding excrement.

Delighting in the acceptance of gifts, having abandoned the wearing of sacred ash, having abandoned the wearing of rudrākṣa beads, having abandoned the vow of the Monday fast, having abandoned the sacrifices to the planets, having abandoned the worship of Viśveśvara,
having abandoned the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra, and having abandoned the worship of Bhairava, [he shall suffer] the terrible tortures of Bhairavī and the like.
Having experienced various kinds of suffering as departed spirits in Kāśī, they then become purified and take refuge in me.
If they discharge semen, urine, or feces inside a house, they thereby sprinkle their ancestors with that [impurity]. Seeing that very evildoer dead, Nīlalohita Bhairava [confronts] him...
He casts [the sinner] into the circle of the sacrificial ground, into blazing pits of fire, and into other such places. Therefore, one should dwell with vigilance;
one should dwell with vigilance in Kāśī, which exists in the form of a Liṅga. This is the Upaniṣad.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O worshipful ones.
With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you; may we attain the lifespan ordained by the gods.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel is uninjured, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace! Hariḥ Oṃ, that is the Truth.
Thus ends the Bhasmajābāla Upaniṣad.
